narration:
The reeds part twenty yards ahead, and the ford opens up: a broad sheet of slow brown water over gravel. Right in the middle of it a cart sits tilted, one wheel sunk to the hub. Beside it a heavyset man in a soaked smock is up to his thighs in the river, shoving at the tailboard and swearing steadily at a grey ox that has planted its feet and is ignoring him.

He's the biggest one there. Rowan goes.

His hand drops to his belt for a blade and closes on nothing. All he has is the cold brass case of his compass. His feet are already moving, though. He comes off the crown of the road and into the shallows, and the river grabs at his shins and slows every step.

The carter turns at the splashing and his face goes slack. He throws up both muddy hands.

"Whoa! *Whoa* — friend, easy! There's nothing on this cart but cheese and butter, and half of it's going off!" The ox bawls.

Behind Rowan and to his left, the reeds rattle. A thin woman stands up out of them without a sound, as if she'd been crouching there all morning. Her shins are black with mud and she has a hooked reed-sickle in one hand. She holds it low and loose, blade down, and doesn't step any closer.

"That's Odo Fenn," she says, flat and unhurried. "He's stuck, not dangerous. Been stuck since first light." Her eyes go over Rowan: his empty hand, his wet boots. "You'd be the first to rob him and come away poorer. Who are you, then?"

Out in the ford, Odo hasn't lowered his hands. Rowan is knee-deep and about ten yards from the cart.

narration:
Rowan pulls up in the knee-deep water and fills his lungs. "The reeve's men are right behind me! You get one chance. Run!"

His voice carries over the water and a pair of ducks bursts out of the reeds downstream. Then the ford goes quiet except for the river.

Odo Fenn looks at him. Then he looks down at his cart, sunk to the hub. Then at the ox, which has chosen this moment to relieve itself in the river.

"*Run?*" His voice cracks. "Friend, I've been trying to leave since first light! If the reeve's sending men, bless every one of them. They can put a shoulder to this wheel." He lowers his hands to chest height, but no further. "And I've done nothing to the reeve, whatever she's told you."

The reed-cutter hasn't moved, except for one eyebrow.

"I've been sat in those reeds since dawn," she says. "That road's soft. Four men in boots, I'd hear them squelch from the hawthorns." She shifts the sickle to her other hand, still blade-down, and steps out onto the gravel at the edge of the water. "So that's no to *who are you*, and a poor lie besides." She doesn't seem angry. If anything, one corner of her mouth has moved.

Odo has seen she isn't afraid, and he gets his nerve back. "Look, whoever you are, you've got two arms. There's coin in it if this wheel comes out before the butter turns."

"There's always coin in it with Odo," the woman says to nobody in particular. "Getting it *out* of him is the trick."

The ox bawls again. Both of them are watching Rowan.

arguments.description: A broad, brown river crossing at the end of the ford road, marked by a line of weathered stakes. The water is running higher on the stakes than the old waterline stains suggest.

arguments.value: The barefoot figure in the reeds is an unlicensed eel-trapper (wiry, middle-aged, called Hobb) checking withy traps staked along the river edge. He hid because he took Rowan for a reeve's man and slipped across the road behind him. He is not hostile, just wary and wants to protect his traps. He knows the ford well: the river is up after rain upstream, and the downstream stakes lean over the deep channel.

The ford is high after rain upstream. It can be crossed with care by reading the stakes and current; a careless crossing risks being swept into the deep channel just downstream. The river is ordinary and nobody sabotaged it.

narration:
The ford road leaves the square between two leaning fence posts and quickly turns to packed mud, rutted by cartwheels and pocked with hoofprints still holding water. Within a few hundred paces the hedges fall away and the reeds rise up on either side, taller than a man, rustling dry at the tops and green lower down. The air smells of silt and cold water. Ahead you can hear the river talking over stones.

You slow down and watch the reed beds instead of the road: the angles of the stalks, the places where they're bent, the gaps where something heavier than wind has pushed through.

narration:
Nothing waits for you on the road ahead. The reeds stand still for twenty paces either way. Then you glance back the way you came, and the road shows you what the reeds didn't. A line of bare footprints crosses the ruts behind you, toes splayed and water still seeping into the heel marks. While you were watching the road ahead, someone stepped out of the left-hand bed and slipped into the right. It happened less than a minute ago.

You go after them. Your hand drops to your belt to draw and closes on the cold brass of the compass. Nothing else is there. You have no knife and no blade. You keep going anyway.

The gap is low and narrow, and the bent stalks point toward the sound of the water. The mud swallows your boots to the ankle. Ten paces in, the reeds open onto a small shelf of silt at the river's edge. A row of wicker eel traps is staked in the shallows. A man crouches over one of them: barefoot, trousers rolled to the knee, wiry as a fence rail, with a short hooked knife for cutting withy ties. Nobody else is here. That makes him the biggest one, and he isn't big.

He hears you a heartbeat late and starts up out of his crouch as you close the distance.

narration:
Your next stride lands on the pale crust of the silt, and the crust gives way. Your boot sinks into black ooze up to the shin, your weight keeps going, and you pitch forward into the shallows. Cold water slaps your face. Something cracks under you: wicker. A whole trap folds flat beneath your hip, the withies snapping like kindling. The compass is in your fist, and your fist is underwater.

The man is already up and three steps back, knife held low, heels at the edge of the reeds. He doesn't come at you. His eyes flick to the gap you came through and the road beyond it.

You get your head out of the water and shout anyway: the reeve's men are right behind you, and this is his one chance to run.

narration:
The ford road leaves the square between low banks, then narrows beside a bed of reeds. Damp ruts hold shallow pools; beyond them comes the steady sound of running water.

Near the first bend, a reed stem snaps. There is little wind. You have not yet rounded the bank, and whoever—or whatever—made the sound is still out of sight.

The reeds show you nothing. Then gravel shifts behind you.

A lean man in a patched coat has stepped onto the road from a drainage hollow you passed. He is only a few paces away, holding an ash cudgel low across his thighs. Mud darkens his knees.

“Stay there.” His voice is quiet, but his grip tightens. “Put your coins down. Walk on to the ford.”

He stands between you and the square. Ahead, the bend offers a way out of his sight, though the rutted ground makes it poor footing for a sprint. He has not closed the distance.

His eyes flick toward your hands. “No trouble, if you don't make any.”

narration:
Your shout carries along the narrow road. The robber’s gaze flicks past you, toward the bend, but his cudgel stays ready.

“The reeve’s men?” He shifts toward the edge of the road. “Then where are their boots?”

He is listening now—for more than your answer.

For several breaths, there is only running water and the faint scrape of reeds.

The robber’s eyes come back to your hands.

“Just you.”

He doesn’t run. Instead, he advances one cautious pace, lifting the cudgel from his thighs. Its reach now covers most of the gap between you.

“Empty your pockets. Slowly.”

The bend toward the ford remains open behind you, but he is watching for a sudden move now.
